item.title: HP 3D Printing - The Inkjet Giant's Ten-Year Manufacturing Bet
item.description: Alex and Jordan profile HP's 3D printing business, from the 2016 Multi Jet Fusion launch with Nike and BMW watching, to a top-tier polymer AM position, a metal binder jetting push, and a decade-old question that still hasn't been answered: is HP's inkjet moat real? Plus the MJF 1200, Craftcloud, and what one reseller exit does and doesn't tell you.

item.title: A Texas Judge, a V8 Block, and Two Imaginary Dimensions
item.description: A federal court strikes down the ATF's ghost gun rule and Alex and Jordan untangle what it actually changes for people who print. Plus: Creality's suspiciously cheap four-color announcement, Bosch and Nikon SLM print a V8 engine block, a two-year-old Indian startup test-fires a printed cryogenic rocket engine, and IBM claims to have invented '5D printing.'

item.title: Creality - The Volume King Trying to Become a Platform
item.description: Alex and Jordan profile Creality, the Shenzhen company whose cheap, hackable Ender-3 put 3D printers on millions of desks. They trace the line from the 2014 CR-3 to high-speed K series machines, a nozzle-changing printer called KliTek, a filament recycler, an e-commerce platform, and the signals that Creality wants to go public.

item.title: The $1.4 Billion Question — Hadrian's Mega-Raise, Hyundai Goes All-In, and Bambu Teases a Laser
item.description: A record-shattering funding round for Hadrian lands with a curious lack of confirmation, Hyundai and Kia open a dedicated additive manufacturing center after 30 years of quiet practice, and Prusa refreshes its whole lineup for free. Plus: a QIDI Plus5 review worth reading, Bambu Lab's mysterious R1 laser teaser, and a 13-year-old in Utah who spent his summer printing a wheelchair for a toddler.

item.title: UltiMaker - The Open Desktop Pioneer Trying to Grow Up Industrial
item.description: Alex and Jordan profile UltiMaker, the company stitched together from two desktop 3D printing pioneers that's now betting on factories, defense, and an open materials ecosystem. From open-source roots and the MakerBot merger to the Factor line and the Bambu Lab squeeze, this is a look at whether a desktop legend can survive by going upmarket.

item.title: The Hospital Is the Factory Now — Walter Reed's FDA First
item.description: Walter Reed becomes the first hospital cleared by the FDA to print its own titanium implants, and Alex and Jordan dig into what it actually takes to turn a medical center into a manufacturer. Plus: Renishaw goes after supports in metal printing, $9 million against the defense qualification wall, a carbon-fiber trick for your desktop prints, and a Florida 3D-printed house that has the New York Post rolling its eyes.

item.title: Materialise: The Company That Bet on Software Before Anyone Knew Software Was the Bet
item.description: Alex and Jordan profile Materialise, the Belgian veteran that decided decades ago that the money in 3D printing wasn't in printers. From Magics and Build Processors to custom PEEK skull implants, they trace how a 1990 founding turned into a dual software-and-medical business, and ask whether a margin-first strategy can survive flat revenue.

item.description: 3DEO, Fusion3, and BigRep all wind down in the same week that Walter Reed lands the first FDA clearance for a hospital-printed cranial implant. item.title: 3D Systems: The Old Guard Bets Everything on Mission-Critical Printing
item.description: Alex and Jordan profile 3D Systems, one of the oldest names in additive manufacturing, as it recasts itself around defense, healthcare, and dental production. From Figure 4 hearing aids to hypersonic metal parts and a Saudi joint venture, the hosts weigh a genuine strategic shift against lawsuits, revenue whiplash, and a leadership picture that's harder to see than it should be.

item.title: The Shakeout Week — BigRep Sold, Würth Closes, and Desktop Metal Hits the Wall

item.title: Bambu Lab - The Walled Garden That Ate Desktop 3D Printing
item.description: We profile Bambu Lab, the company that turned 'it just works' into a market-leading strategy for desktop 3D printing. From the X1 Carbon to an integrated ecosystem, a Stratasys lawsuit, and an open-source backlash, we sort what's confirmed from what's hype - including a valuation rumor that does not survive contact with reality.

item.title: Bioprinting Goes to Orbit — and the 20-Second Miracle
item.description: Auxilium says it bioprinted kidney and liver tissue on the ISS — we dig into what that actually proves. Plus Venus Aerospace's $91M detonation-engine round, Framatome's nuclear WAAM center, DAIHEN and EOS on the materials front, a clever single-AMS color trick, and a University of Utah claim that objects can print in a single 20-second laser shot.

item.title: Stratasys: The FDM Founder Trying to Become an Industrial Company
item.description: We profile Stratasys, the 35-year-old company that invented FDM and now sits in the middle of a high-stakes pivot from prototyping to serial production. item.title: Stratasys Buys Markforged for a Song, and a $185K Metal Printer
item.description: Alex and Jordan dig into the biggest AM deal of the year—Stratasys snapping up Markforged for just $42.5 million, minus the metal binder jet line. They also unpack a new dual-laser metal printer priced suspiciously low, Norsk Titanium's first real production contract with Northrop Grumman, and whether an AI that fixes prints mid-job is ready for your garage.
